title: First Nations Use of Plant & Animal Adaptations
subtitle: How knowing an adaptation turns it into food, medicine and tools
subject: Biology
syllabusDotPoints: Explain how Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples use the adaptations of local plants and animals for specific purposes
lessonIntent: Students can explain how Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples use specific adaptations of local plants and animals for specific purposes, linking each use to the underlying structural, physiological or behavioural adaptation.
examSkill: Name the adaptation, classify it, and explain what understanding it made possible, citing the People and Country the example belongs to.

introVoiceover.text: Welcome to HSC Science. This is HSC Biology. Today, First Nations use of plant and animal adaptations. Let's get into it.

scenes.caption: First Nations use of plant and animal adaptations

scenes.heading: How do you make a toxic seed safe to eat?
scenes.body: Macrozamia cycad seeds are packed with starch, and with toxins the plant makes to stop seed-eaters. Aboriginal Peoples turned them into a safe, storable staple.
scenes.callout: How does a plant's defence become food, or a fishing tool, and what did people need to know?
scenes.caption: Plant and animal adaptations, put to specific purposes.

voiceover.text: Here's a puzzle. Macrozamia cycad seeds are packed with starch, but they're also toxic. The plant makes those toxins as a defence, to stop animals eating its seeds. Yet Aboriginal Peoples across northern and eastern Australia turned them into a safe, storable staple food. Another plant's defence chemical became a fishing tool. So how does a plant's adaptation, which exists for the plant's own survival, get put to a human purpose? And what did people need to know to do it? That's today's lesson.

scenes.heading: Knowledge built on Country
scenes.body: Using an adaptation starts with understanding it: what the feature does for the organism, and how it works.

bullets.text: Country: the land, waters and skies a group belongs to, with the knowledge and responsibilities tied to them.
First Nations knowledge: detailed, place-based knowledge of species, developed and passed on over many thousands of years.
Plant secondary compound: a chemical such as a toxin that a plant makes as a defence, a physiological adaptation.
Seasonal indicator: a reliable natural sign that tells you another event is due.

scenes.callout: Empirical, tested across generations, and specific to each Country.
scenes.caption: Country, First Nations knowledge, secondary compound, seasonal indicator.

voiceover.text: Let's set up the language. Country means the land, waters and skies a group belongs to, and the knowledge and responsibilities tied to them. First Nations knowledge of species is detailed and place-based, built from repeated observation over many thousands of years, and specific to each Country. A plant secondary compound is a chemical, like a toxin, that a plant makes as a defence. And a seasonal indicator is a reliable natural sign that another event is due. One more thing. Today's examples are published and cited. Much knowledge is held by particular communities, and isn't ours to repeat.

scenes.heading: Plant defences, put to a purpose
scenes.body: A plant defence can also become a resource when people know how to manage it safely.

bullets.text: Macrozamia communis (burrawang) produces starch-rich seeds that are poisonous without careful processing.
Wreck Bay community knowledge documented by the Australian National Botanic Gardens describes placing the seeds in creek water so running water leaches them before use.
The biological link: chemical defence deters consumers; cultural processing works around that defence to make the food resource usable.

scenes.secondary: Source trail: Australian National Botanic Gardens, Aboriginal Plant Use — Macrozamia communis, citing Wreck Bay Community & Renwick (2000).
scenes.callout: Name the plant adaptation, then explain how community knowledge makes safe use possible.
scenes.caption: Burrawang seeds: plant chemical defence, with community-documented processing to make them usable as food.

voiceover.text: For a plant example, use one with a clear source trail. Macrozamia communis, or burrawang, produces starch-rich seeds that are poisonous without careful processing. The Australian National Botanic Gardens records Wreck Bay community knowledge describing the seeds being placed in creek water so running water could leach them before use. Biologically, the plant's chemical defence discourages consumers. The cultural response is knowledge of how to process the seed safely enough to use the large food resource. Keep the community attribution with the example rather than presenting the practice as generic.

scenes.heading: Reading animal behaviour
scenes.body: Knowing an animal's behavioural adaptation, its migration or its timing, tells you when and where it can be reliably harvested.

bullets.text: Short-finned eels are catadromous: they migrate downstream to the sea to spawn. Gunditjmara engineering at Budj Bim used channels, weirs and holding ponds to intercept and hold eels.

At Masig in the Torres Strait, Masigalgal seasonal knowledge links the start of Sulawal turtle mating with local seasonal indicators, including ripening Kubil Gim fruit and Biru Biru bee-eater migration.

scenes.secondary: Source trail: Budj Bim Cultural Landscape — Gunditjmara community/UNESCO documentation. Masig example — Masigalgal RNTBC and Masigalgal Rangers seasonal calendar, published with the Bureau of Meteorology (2018).
scenes.callout: Community knowledge links predictable biological timing to sustainable use and management.
scenes.caption: Gunditjmara eel systems at Budj Bim; Masigalgal seasonal knowledge on Masig in the Torres Strait.

voiceover.text: Animal behaviour and seasonal timing can make a resource predictable. On Gunditjmara Country at Budj Bim, short-finned eels migrate through waterways on their way to the sea to spawn. Channels, weirs and holding ponds were engineered around that movement so eels could be trapped and kept alive. For a distinct Torres Strait Islander example, the Masigalgal seasonal calendar for Masig records community knowledge of Sulawal turtle mating and the environmental signs that accompany it, including ripening Kubil Gim fruit and the arrival of Biru Biru bee-eaters. These examples should be taught with their named community sources, not as generic First Nations knowledge.

rows.name: Sulawal turtle

scenes.heading: Reading the calendar the environment writes
scenes.body: Seasonal calendars are community knowledge systems that record natural indicators of changing seasons and resource timing.

bullets.text: Masigalgal people of Masig in the Torres Strait developed a community-led seasonal calendar with elders and rangers.
In Naigai season, ripening Kubil Gim (Sea Ebony) fruit and Biru Biru bee-eater migration are indicators associated with the start of Sulawal turtle mating.
The indicator does not cause the animal event; both reflect seasonal environmental conditions observed over generations.

scenes.callout: Attribute cultural knowledge to the community that owns and documents it.
scenes.caption: Masig seasonal calendar: Masigalgal indicators connect seasonal change with Sulawal turtle mating.

voiceover.text: Seasonal calendars are not generic lists of signs; they are community knowledge systems tied to Country and Sea Country. On Masig in the Torres Strait, Masigalgal elders and rangers developed a seasonal calendar through a community-led project. In the Naigai season, the calendar records signs including ripening Kubil Gim, or Sea Ebony, fruit and the migration of Biru Biru bee-eaters alongside the start of Sulawal turtle mating. The sign does not cause the turtle behaviour. The value is the long-observed relationship between several biological and environmental events. Always attribute this knowledge to the Masigalgal community source.

scenes.secondary: Source: Masigalgal RNTBC and Masigalgal Rangers, Masig seasonal calendar; Bureau of Meteorology Indigenous Weather Knowledge, 2018.

scenes.heading: Analyse Budj Bim
scenes.question: Analyse how Gunditjmara knowledge of the short-finned eel's migration made the Budj Bim aquaculture system possible.
scenes.coachNote: Link each structure to a feature of the behaviour: numbers, route, timing.
steps: Adaptation: short-finned eels are catadromous, migrating downstream to the sea to spawn, in large numbers, along water courses, at predictable times.
Knowing where and when they move turns a mobile resource into a predictable one, and a predictable resource can be engineered for.
Channels intercepted the route, weirs controlled the flow, and holding ponds kept the eels alive once trapped.
Holding them alive turned a seasonal run into a year-round food supply: aquaculture, not just fishing.
Answer: the system is built around the behaviour, and its age (at least about 6,600 years) shows knowledge accumulated and refined ✓
scenes.caption: Every part of Budj Bim is matched to a feature of the eel migration.

voiceover.text: Let's analyse Budj Bim, the way an exam wants it. Start with the adaptation. Short-finned eels are catadromous, migrating downstream to the sea to spawn, in large numbers, along water courses, at predictable times. Next, what knowing that makes possible. If you know where and when the eels will move, a mobile resource becomes a predictable one, and you can build for it. Then match each structure to the behaviour. Channels intercepted the route. Weirs controlled the flow. Holding ponds kept the eels alive once trapped. And that's the decisive part. Holding them alive turns one seasonal run into a year-round food supply. That's aquaculture, not just catching fish. Finally, the age of the system, thousands of years, shows knowledge built up and refined over generations.

scenes.heading: It wasn't trial and error
scenes.body: Wrong: using plants and animals was simple trial and error, or "folklore".
scenes.secondary: Right: it is an empirical knowledge system, built from repeated observation over tens of thousands of years and specific to each Country. Knowing which species, which part, how to prepare it and when it is available is deep biological understanding.
scenes.mistakeTag: Name the People and the Country
scenes.callout: Never write "Aboriginal people used", as if the whole continent held one set of practices.
scenes.caption: An empirical, place-based knowledge system, not guesswork.

voiceover.text: Here's the misconception this lesson is built to fix. Describing this knowledge as simple trial and error, or folklore. It's an empirical knowledge system, built from repeated observation over tens of thousands of years, and tested across generations. Look at what the cycad needs. You have to know which part is toxic, what removes the toxin, and how long the treatment must run. That's detailed biology. And a writing habit that matters. Name the People and the Country, and cite where you read it. Never write Aboriginal people used, as if the whole continent held one set of practices. The species, the seasons and the methods differ from Country to Country.

scenes.heading: Quick check
scenes.question: Macrozamia seeds contain cycasin and macrozamin, yet were processed into a staple food. Identify the adaptation being used, classify it, and say what the processing shows.
scenes.pausePrompt: Pause: is the adaptation the toxin, or the leaching?
answerSteps: The adaptation is the toxin: a chemical defence against seed predators.
Making a defensive chemical is an internal process, so it is physiological.
The leaching, or ageing and fermenting, is the human response to it.
Answer: it shows people knew the toxin could be removed, from which part, and for how long ✓
scenes.caption: The toxin is the adaptation; the leaching is the human response.

voiceover.text: Quick check. Macrozamia seeds contain toxins called cycasin and macrozamin, yet they were processed into a staple food. Identify the adaptation being used, classify it, and say what the processing shows. Careful, is the adaptation the toxin, or the leaching? Pause and decide. Right. The adaptation is the toxin, a chemical defence the plant makes against seed predators. Making a chemical is an internal process, so it's a physiological adaptation. The leaching, or the ageing and fermenting, isn't an adaptation at all. It's the human response to one. And what does it show? That people knew the toxin could be removed, which part carries it, and how long treatment has to run, before the seed is safe.

scenes.heading: Lock it in
points: Every adaptation exists for the organism; knowing why it has the feature is what makes it usable.
Plant defences: Tephrosia to harvest fish; Macrozamia seeds leached into a staple food.
Animal behaviour: Bogong moth aestivation in the Alps; eel migration at Budj Bim.
Seasonal indicators work because two species respond to the same cue.
Name the People and Country, cite the source, and treat it as empirical knowledge.
scenes.finalPrompt: For any use: name the adaptation, classify it, then say what had to be known.
scenes.caption: Five takeaways on First Nations use of adaptations.

voiceover.text: Let's lock it in. Every adaptation exists for the organism's own survival, and knowing why it has the feature is what makes it usable. Plant defences were put to work, Tephrosia to harvest fish, and Macrozamia seeds leached into a staple food. Animal behaviour was read, the Bogong moth's summer in the Alps, and the eel migration engineered around at Budj Bim. Seasonal indicators work because two species respond to the same cue. And always name the People and the Country, and cite your source. For any example, name the adaptation, classify it, then say what had to be known.
